targetAudience.primary: Enterprise architects, security engineers and governance leads responsible for agent connectors
targetAudience.knowledgeAssumption: The reader understands connectors, linked accounts, runtime policy and provider permissions.
targetAudience.readerProblem: An Installed or Enabled connector can be mistaken for proof that a specific call is currently authorized.

whyNow: Current first-party documentation and implementation evidence expose different authority layers across Epic integrations, Entra Agent IDs and Codex application-tool policy evaluation.

externalHook.description: One visible Enabled state can hide the acting account, target permission, runtime policy and provider effect.

coreProposition: Connector governance must keep administrative availability, configured capability, acting principal/account, target-resource permission, runtime policy and provider effect evidence separate; installation or enablement cannot authorize a call by itself.

originalValue.description: Synthesizes three non-equivalent product samples into a bounded call-admission and audit model without claiming a universal protocol.

readerTakeaway: Treat Installed and Enabled as capability signals; admit each call only when principal, account link, target scope and runtime policy are current, then record provider effects separately.

supported: OpenAI Epic documentation separates setup and scopes from clinician sign-in and existing patient-chart permissions.
Microsoft documents configured connector permissions with runtime connector-policy and DLP revalidation.
The cited Codex revision passes selected account-link and tool information into application-tool policy evaluation.
uncertain: When permission changes require explicit reapproval

firstPartyRole.rationale: The article compares general authority layers across documented systems.

decisionReason: The sources expose complementary failure boundaries and support an independently useful six-layer authority model.
